claim.pdf_says: 15.4   Returned values  ...  15.4.1   Numeric and integer functions
claim.markdown_says: `## 15.4 Returned values` immediately followed by `## 15.4.1 Numeric and integer functions` — both level 2
claim.why_it_matters: 15.4.1 is emitted at the same markdown level as its parent 15.4, so it renders as a peer clause rather than a subclause. The parallel construction two clauses later is transcribed correctly (`## 15.5 Date and time conversion functions` / `### 15.5.1 General`), which shows the intended convention.

verdict.reasoning:
REFUTED on three independent grounds.

(1) NOTHING IS MISSING. The claim is filed as kind=missing-heading, but both headings are present in the transcription with byte-exact text and byte-exact numbering. Rendered PDF page 834 (printed folio 804) prints exactly two headings: '15.4   Returned values' and '15.4.1   Numeric and integer functions'. page-834.md line 13 has '## 15.4 Returned values' and line 18 has '## 15.4.1 Numeric and integer functions'; specs/ISO_COBOL.md carries the same at lines 33659 and 33664, each with a correct anchor (`section-15-4`, `section-15-4-1`). The only thing at issue is the count of '#' characters. (Minor misquote in the claim: the two headings are not 'immediately' adjacent — the 15.4 body paragraph ending '...as specified in 15.2, Types of functions.' sits between them, correctly transcribed.)

(2) THE PDF CARRIES NO LEVEL DISTINCTION TO LOSE. I cropped both headings from the 300dpi render and compared them side by side at 2x magnification. They are typographically IDENTICAL: same bold serif face, same point size (cap-height measured equal), same left margin (both flush at the body-text left edge), same tab gap between number and title. ISO/IEC 1989:2023 does not size-differentiate clause from subclause headings at this depth. There is therefore no property of the source document that the markdown fails to reproduce. The sole depth signal the PDF emits is the dotted number itself — '15.4.1' — and the transcription reproduces that verbatim. A reader or a citation tool reading '15.4.1' knows unambiguously it is a subclause of 15.4.

(3) THE ALLEGED 'INTENDED CONVENTION' DOES NOT EXIST. This is the claim's load-bearing evidence and it does not survive checking. I extracted every clause-15 heading in specs/ISO_COBOL.md with its level and its numbering depth. Of 32 headings, only the first four satisfy level == depth+1; every heading from 15.3.1 onward violates it:
  ### 15.1 / ### 15.2 / ### 15.3        (2-part numbers at level 3)
  ## 15.3.1                              (3-part at level 2)
  ### 15.3.1.1 ... ### 15.3.1.4          (4-part at level 3)
  ## 15.3.1.5 / ## 15.3.1.6 / ## 15.3.1.7 (4-part at level 2)
  ## 15.3.2 / ## 15.3.3                  (3-part at level 2)
  ## 15.3.3.6.1                          (5-part at level 2)
  ## 15.5.3 / ## 15.5.4 / ## 15.5.5      (3-part at level 2)
The claim cites '## 15.5' + '### 15.5.1' as proof of convention, but the very next siblings — 15.5.3, 15.5.4, 15.5.5 — are emitted at '##', i.e. at the same level as their parent 15.5, which is precisely the pattern the claim calls a defect. The cited pair is a cherry-pick from a two-value distribution, not a convention. Note also that the top-level clauses themselves disagree with each other: 15.1/15.2/15.3 are '###' while 15.4/15.5/15.6/15.7 are '##'. Under the claim's own rule, 15.1 would be a subclause of 15 and 15.4 would be a peer of 15.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY GOING ON: heading level in this transcription tracks page-render artifacts, not document structure — the level flips at page boundaries (p829 and p831 and p835 emit level-2 first then level-3; p830, p832, p834, p836 emit level-2 throughout) regardless of numbering depth. That is the expected failure mode of a font-metric heuristic applied to a document whose clause and subclause headings are set in the same font at the same size, which is exactly what finding (2) established. It is a global property of the extraction pipeline affecting hundreds of headings across the document, not a page-834 PDF-vs-markdown discrepancy.

DISPOSITION: no content is missing, no text is misquoted from the PDF, no meaning is changed, and the normative depth indicator (the dotted clause number) is intact. Per the rejection criteria this is formatting-only. If the owner wants depth-encoded heading levels, that is a single mechanical document-wide pass derivable from the clause numbers already present — a tooling improvement, not a spec-reconciliation finding, and it must not be logged as a page-834 defect.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a discrepancy. Both headings are present on page 834 with exact text and exact ISO numbering ('15.4 Returned values', '15.4.1 Numeric and integer functions'); nothing is missing, so kind=missing-heading is inapplicable. The PDF prints the two headings in identical bold face, identical point size and identical left margin — verified by direct pixel comparison of the 300dpi render — so the source encodes hierarchy only via the dotted clause number, which the markdown reproduces verbatim. The claim's supporting premise is false: markdown heading level does not encode numbering depth anywhere in clause 15 (e.g. '### 15.1', '## 15.3.1', '### 15.3.1.1', '## 15.3.3.6.1', and '## 15.5.3'/'## 15.5.4'/'## 15.5.5' sitting at the same level as their parent '## 15.5' — the identical pattern the claim flags as a defect two clauses earlier). Heading level in this transcription varies with page-render artifacts rather than structure. If depth-encoded levels are wanted, that is a document-wide mechanical normalization pass over the existing clause numbers, not a page-834 finding.
